extracted.intended_audience: social media users, digital marketers, educators, and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forming, using, and managing hashtags across social platforms, including format rules, platform-specific behaviours, etiquette, and functions such as searchability, activism, marketing, and sentiment expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtag format requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A hashtag must begin with a hash (#) character followed by other characters, and is terminated by a space or the end of the line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some platforms may require the # to be preceded with a space. Platforms differ in exact termination rules; treat whitespace or line end as delimiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed characters in hashtags
rubrics_metrics.description: Most or all platforms that support hashtags permit the inclusion of letters (without diacritics), numerals, and underscores. Other characters may be supported on a platform-by-platform basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some characters (for example '&') are generally not supported because they serve other search functions. Check platform-specific documentation for edge cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case sensitivity and legibility (CamelCase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags are not case sensitive (a search for "#hashtag" will match "#HashTag").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using embedded capitals (CamelCase) increases legibility and improves accessibility (e.g., screen readers can better parse #SaveTheDay vs #savetheday).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language-specific handling and scripts without word dividers
rubrics_metrics.description: Languages that do not use word dividers handle hashtags differently (e.g., Sina Weibo/Tencent Weibo use #HashName# format; Twitter may use unspaced characters separated by spaces or zero-width non-joiner characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working in Chinese, Japanese, or other scripts without spacing, follow platform conventions (double-hash delimiters, zero-width non-joiners) to keep hashtags readable and properly delimited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific variations and features
rubrics_metrics.description: Different platforms treat hashtags differently (e.g., Twitter hyperlinks all hashtags to search results; Twitter introduced Trending Topics; World Cup used temporary 'hashflags').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design hashtag strategy with platform features in mind (trending algorithms, hyperlinking, hashflags, regional language support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and community rules (etiquette and regulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some communities may limit, officially or unofficially, the number of hashtags permitted on a single post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive or unrelated use of hashtags can have consequences: Twitter warns that adding hashtags to unrelated tweets or repeating the same hashtag without contributing can filter an account from search results or lead to suspension. Follow each community's etiquette to avoid penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtag deactivation and moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual platforms may deactivate certain hashtags either for being too generic to be useful or due to their use to facilitate illegal activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on extremely generic hashtags that platforms may block or de-emphasize (e.g., #photography on Instagram). Monitor hashtag availability and platform moderation actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing wording for event hashtags (avoid generic collisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags intended for discussion of a particular event tend to use an obscure wording to avoid being caught up with generic conversations on similar subjects (e.g., use #cakefestival rather than #cake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscure wording reduces noise but can hinder adoption; balancing uniqueness with recognizability is necessary. For topics to trend there must be consensus that the hashtag refers to that specific topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtags as unregistered, mutable metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags are neither registered nor controlled by any one user or group. They do not contain set definitions, meaning one hashtag can be used for many purposes and accepted meaning can change over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect ambiguity and possible meaning shifts; coordinate and communicate hashtag intent when organizing events or campaigns to build consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtags for searchability and cross-referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: On social media, hashtags are used as a form of user-generated tagging that enables cross-referencing of content by topic or theme and helps users find content of similar interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hashtags to make content discoverable in unmoderated forums lacking formal ontology; align tags with audience search habits and existing tag conventions to increase reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtags as meta-commentary and expressive devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags may be used informally to express context around a message with no intent to categorize for later searching; they can serve as reflexive meta-commentary or to express emotion (e.g., #toomuchfaketan, #sarcasm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such expressive hashtags for tone and context, but be aware they may not aid discoverability and can be interpreted differently by readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtags and sentiment/sarcasm detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in hashtags are strong predictors of whether a statement is sarcastic; hashtag content reveals sentiment the author attaches to a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers and practitioners doing sentiment analysis should account for hashtags as high-value features, especially for sarcasm detection—this is a known difficult AI problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of alternative tag conventions (cashtags/tickers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate formats exist, such as ticker symbols preceded by the dollar sign (e.g., $XRX), known as 'cashtags'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cashtags are used for financial tagging (stock symbols, currencies) and have platform-specific adoption (e.g., StockTwits, Cash App). Use the appropriate convention for domain-specific tagging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial and branded hashtag usage (co-optation by industries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies, businesses, and advocacy organizations use hashtags for promotion; television broadcasters and advertisers add hashtags to encourage viewer participation and backchannel discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Branded hashtags can boost engagement but risk hijacking or critical responses (example: McDonald's #McDStories). Plan moderation and crisis response when promoting branded tags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hashtags in activism and political mobilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags have played critical roles in social movements (e.g., #jesuischarlie, #BLM, #MeToo) by spreading awareness and organizing discussions across countries and languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hashtag activism can amplify voices and enable storytelling but faces challenges such as noise, hate, disengagement, and the need for sustaining consensus. Consider privacy, safety, and moderation implications for vulnerable users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational and professional development use
rubrics_metrics.description: Hashtags play an important role for employees and students in professional fields and education, enabling community-building and sharing of resources (e.g., #MFLtwitterati for language teachers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using hashtags strategically can support professional learning communities and pedagogical resource-sharing; research shows positive impacts on teaching strategies and student engagement in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic/structural properties of hashtags
rubrics_metrics.description: Some linguists argue hashtagging is a morphological process and that hashtags function as words; popularity is influenced by preexisting popular hashtags with similar syntactic formats (viral hashtags serve as blueprints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating hashtags, consider syntactic patterns of successful tags—conciseness, syntax, and resemblance to viral formats can influence adoption more than mere clarity.
